analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare offer its own drug plan and negotiate prescription prices directly with drug makers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after being introduced with 9 House Democrats behind it, it sat in two committees until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a government-run Medicare prescription drug plan, offered nationwide alongside the private drug plans seniors can choose today. The government plan would negotiate prices directly with drug manufacturers and use a tested formulary to steer patients to drugs that work as well for less. It would also set up a clear appeal process for beneficiaries denied a non-formulary drug they need.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who pay Part D premiums and drug copays. A Medicare-operated plan negotiating directly with manufacturers could lower drug prices and premiums, and the appeals process would help people who get denied a medically necessary drug. Seniors would gain a new choice: a public plan competing with the private drug plans on the market.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer one or more Medicare-operated prescription drug plans with nationwide service areas, giving beneficiaries a public option alongside private Part D plans.

Requires the Secretary to negotiate directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers over purchase prices for the Medicare-operated plan, overturning the current law that bars Medicare from negotiating drug prices, and to use strategies similar to other federal purchasers such as the VA.

Directs the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality to assess drugs' clinical benefit and safety so the plan's formulary rewards drugs that cost less and work better, with tiered copays, reference pricing, and generic substitution as tools.

Requires an appeals process for beneficiaries denied a non-formulary drug, including an external review by an independent entity when medically necessary, developed in consultation with consumer and patient groups.
Guarantees the public plan meets the same pharmacy-access requirements that apply to private drug plans.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face a buyer with real negotiating power over the purchase prices of drugs covered by Medicare Part D. Private insurers that sell standalone Part D drug plans would also face a new government-run competitor.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: A government plan with formulary incentives like prior authorization, step therapy, and reference pricing could limit some beneficiaries' access to specific brand-name drugs, a restriction private plans already use but which opponents say is harder to escape when the government is the plan.

The bill's own text allowed the public plan to begin in 2012 while the bill was written in 2013, a drafting mismatch that signals the plan was modeled on an earlier proposal rather than carefully tailored to this Congress.

Private Part D insurers argue that government negotiates on behalf of millions of beneficiaries and could use its market power to push prices below what a fair market would bear, threatening investment in new medicines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is potentially large and concrete: seniors would get a plan that negotiates drug prices the way the VA does, at a time when Medicare was legally barred from doing so, plus a real appeal process for coverage denials. The cost falls almost entirely on pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose prices under Part D would face downward pressure. The main design risk is that a formulary-driven public plan restricts some drug choices, though it would be constrained to clinically justified limits and required to meet the same pharmacy-access rules as private plans. On balance the benefits to Medicare beneficiaries outweigh the drawbacks.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, and neither committee ever took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on February 28, 2013, joined by Reps. Farr, Lee of California, George Miller of California, and Pingree as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to two committees with jurisdiction over Medicare — Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means — and within days was referred to the health subcommittees of each.

No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed; the last recorded action was the March 7, 2013 referral to a Subcommittee on Health, and the bill died at the end of the 113th Congress in January 2015.
All nine sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and with Republicans controlling the House and its committees, the bill never moved past the referral stage.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical makers and private insurers that sell Medicare Part D plans came out ahead: Medicare kept the current law barring it from negotiating drug prices, and no government-run competitor plan was created. Seniors continued paying market-set Part D drug prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and Part D insurers

sides.party_line_note: All 9 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and with Republicans holding the House majority and chairing both committees of referral, the bill's movement depended entirely on the majority party, which took no action.

industries.note: The bill would require the Secretary to negotiate purchase prices for the public plan, applying pressure that private Part D plans currently absorb through middlemen. Current law bars Medicare from negotiating drug prices, so manufacturers' Part D revenue was protected by the status quo this bill attacked. The industry's interest in keeping prices set by market forces runs directly against beneficiaries' interest in lower drug costs.

A Medicare-operated drug plan offered nationwide would be a direct government competitor for the millions of seniors enrolled in private drug plans. The public plan would also benefit from negotiated purchase prices private plans cannot obtain, though the bill requires it to meet the same operational rules as private plans.

The bill's formulary strategy encourages generic substitution and requires the plan to meet the same pharmacy-access standards as private plans, so dispensing pharmacies and generic manufacturers would likely gain volume as cheaper drugs were steered toward patients.
